provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: In the original task, a gray (5) line runs along the main diagonal. Every coloured cell below that line moves to its mirror position across the line. This is the same as transposing the grid. Under a D4 transform, a mirror across a diagonal turns into a mirror across the image of that diagonal. The factory works out which diagonal the gray line lands on. A row reversal (d4>=4) moves the main diagonal to the anti-diagonal, and each clockwise rotation swaps the main and anti-diagonals. So the line is the anti-diagonal exactly when (flip + d4%4) is odd. The emitted program works directly in visible coordinates and follows the same staged mechanism as the rule: it clears every non-background cell off the line, then redraws each one at its mirror position. For the main diagonal, (r,c) maps to (c,r). For the anti-diagonal, (r,c) maps to (n-1-c, n-1-r). Gray cells on the line stay fixed. The background is the constant palette[0]. Colours are never permuted, because the mirror only moves pixels.
draft_notes.limitations: No tests have been run. The program assumes the generator's domain: square grids with the gray line on the visible diagonal determined by d4, and the opposite half empty in the input. On that domain, clearing and redrawing gives exactly the full reflection. Two edge cases are handled defensively rather than by the true rule: non-square inputs fall back to the leading square, and if both halves held colours, overlapping writes would favour later cells in row-major order. Constructor note: the archived transform computes an object-wise canvas, then discards it and returns g.T. The two agree on this domain, so this is not a labelling defect. No fixture contradicts the uniform mirror rule.
